problems.stem: A software audit recommends Tool A because "it has 30 features versus Tool B's 12." What is wrong with this conclusion?
options: Thirty features is too many for any learning tool.
It counts features rather than fit; the audit never asks which features actually serve the defined learning task.
Tool B should win because simpler is always better.
Feature counts are fine as long as both numbers are verified.
problems.explanation: A comparative audit judges fit to the task. A long feature list can include capabilities irrelevant to the learning goal.

problems.stem: An audit praises Tool A for low price and Tool B for strong accessibility, then picks Tool A. Why is the comparison unsound?
options: Price should never be an audit criterion.
The tools were scored on different axes, so no head-to-head judgment was made; each must be scored on the same shared criteria set.
Tool B should automatically win on accessibility alone.
Two criteria are too few for any audit.
problems.explanation: A real comparison requires one common criteria set applied to every tool. Praising each on a different dimension prevents an actual head-to-head verdict.

problems.stem: An audit concludes "Tool C is the best authoring tool." What does a defensible audit add to that claim?
options: A trophy graphic to emphasize the winner.
The context the recommendation assumes: the learners, setting, budget, and constraints under which Tool C wins, so a reader knows when the verdict would change.
A statement that Tool C is best for everyone everywhere.
The release date of Tool C.
problems.explanation: There is no context-free best tool. Naming the assumed learners, setting, and constraints makes the recommendation falsifiable and transferable.

problems.stem: Your audit scored three tools on the same five criteria and Tool B won overall but failed the accessibility criterion outright. What is the strongest evidence-based revision to the recommendation?
options: Keep Tool B as the flat winner because it had the best total score.

Flag accessibility as a non-negotiable gate: if your learners include screen-reader users, Tool B is disqualified despite its total, and the recommendation shifts to the next tool that passes the gate.
Drop the accessibility criterion so Tool B can win cleanly.
Average the scores again to smooth out the accessibility failure.
problems.explanation: Some criteria are gates, not weights. A defensible audit lets a non-negotiable failure override a high total when the context requires it.
